solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Grabbed time to tour quiet Asian city

indicators.note: to tour a place is to travel all round it, so the outer letters go round something

parts.note: grabbed means taken, past participle
T is the standard abbreviation for time
sh! is the call for quiet

explanation.surface: A traveller seized the chance to visit a peaceful city in Asia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grabbed time' reads as seizing a moment, but the two words simply supply letters that are then split to wrap the quiet signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Tashkent is the capital of Uzbekistan in Central Asia, so it is an example of a city on that continent.

clue.text: Unlikely I felt that this might be wicked

parts.note: a tall story is an unlikely one
the cry you give when something hurts

explanation.surface: Someone doubts they could ever feel a thing might be evil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wicked' looks like 'evil', but here it means 'fitted with a wick'. TALL as in a tall tale; OW as in the yelp of pain.
explanation.definitionFit: Tallow is rendered animal fat once used for making candles, and candles are given wicks, so tallow might be wicked.

clue.text: Glad as bed is moved, revealing pouch by seat

indicators.note: things that are moved get put in new positions, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters used as they stand

explanation.surface: Someone is pleased when their bed is shifted to reveal a pouch hidden by a chair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Glad' reads as the mood of the sentence, but it is just letters to rearrange along with 'as bed'.
explanation.definitionFit: A saddlebag is a bag hung from a saddle, the seat of a horse or bicycle, so it is a pouch beside a seat.

clue.text: Arab nation reversed hold on island

indicators.note: something reversed is turned back to front, so its letters are read the other way

parts.note: the United Kingdom, a nation
to pause before acting, as when told to hang on a moment
I is the abbreviation for island

explanation.surface: An Arab country has backed away from its grip on an island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arab nation' reads as one phrase, but 'Arab' alone is the definition and 'nation' is UK.
explanation.definitionFit: A Kuwaiti is a person from Kuwait, an Arab state on the Gulf, so a Kuwaiti is one kind of Arab.

clue.text: Two centuries back, hotel becoming nick

indicators.note: going back means travelling the other way, so the letters are read from the end

parts.note: C and TON are two ways of writing a hundred
H is hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Two hundred years ago a hotel was turned into a police station.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Two centuries back' reads as two hundred years ago, but it is two words for a hundred, C and TON, turned round. Nick is British slang for a police station, the false trail.
explanation.definitionFit: A notch is a small cut in an edge, and a nick is exactly that sort of small cut.

clue.text: Impulsive military assistant's cracking plan

indicators.note: to crack something is to break into it, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a map is a plan of an area
an aide-de-camp is an officer's assistant

explanation.surface: A rash officer's aide has worked out a scheme.
explanation.walkthrough: ADC is the usual abbreviation for aide-de-camp. 'Cracking' sounds like 'excellent' or 'solving', but it means breaking into.
explanation.definitionFit: Madcap describes someone reckless and acting on sudden whims, which is what impulsive means.

clue.text: Paciest bowling to become sterile

indicators.note: bowling things along sends them rolling and tumbling, so the letters are tumbled into a new order

parts.note: the letters used as they stand

explanation.surface: The fastest bowler in cricket ends up being ineffective.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket picture makes 'bowling' a sporting action, but it is the signal to reorder the letters of 'Paciest'.
explanation.definitionFit: Aseptic means free from bacteria and germs, as in a surgical setting, which is the medical sense of sterile.

clue.text: Not exactly a shock for one getting behind supporter

indicators.note: getting behind means coming after, so one piece follows the other

parts.note: C is circa, Latin for about
a shock of hair is a thick mass of it

explanation.surface: A fan backing their team gets something less than a real fright.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shock' suggests a fright, but a shock is a mop of hair. C (circa) is the dating abbreviation meaning roughly.
explanation.definitionFit: A chair is furniture that holds up the person sitting in it, so it is a literal supporter.

clue.text: Means to convey fuel policy after tweet

indicators.note: one item placed after another sits next in line behind it

parts.note: to pipe is to make a high bird-like sound
a party line is its policy

explanation.surface: An energy policy is announced on social media.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tweet' suggests a social media post, but it is the bird's call, PIPE.
explanation.definitionFit: A pipeline is a long run of pipes carrying oil or gas over distance, a way of transporting fuel.

clue.text: Worried about brief to offer one present

indicators.note: something brief is cut short, so the final letter goes
about means round the outside, so one piece wraps another

parts.note: worried, as in what's eating you
to tender is to offer, with its last letter dropped

explanation.surface: Someone is anxious about a short gift for a party guest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Present' looks like a gift but means being there. ATE for worried comes from 'eaten up with worry'.
explanation.definitionFit: An attendee is a person who goes to a meeting or event, someone who is there in person.

clue.text: Old nurse had my pill that we must dissolve

indicators.note: a thing that dissolves breaks up and loses its form, so the letters lose their order

parts.note: the letters used as they stand

explanation.surface: An elderly nurse hands over a tablet that the patients are told to let melt.
explanation.walkthrough: The pill that must dissolve fits the nursing picture, which is why the anagram signal hides so well.
explanation.definitionFit: Florence Nightingale, the Victorian nursing pioneer of the Crimean War, was nicknamed the Lady with the Lamp.

clue.text: Well endowed?

parts.note: surface reading: generously built or well provided for
setter's reading: an oil well, so endowed with plenty of that fuel

explanation.walkthrough: 'Well' looks like an adverb but is the noun: a well drilled for crude, and a country blessed with many of them.
explanation.definitionFit: A nation with vast petroleum reserves is called oil-rich, endowed with wealth from its wells.

clue.text: Hospital department personnel, half in need of case or grip

parts.note: ear, nose and throat department
human resources

indicators.note: lacking a case means having no outer covering, so only the inside letters remain

parts.note: the word without its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A hospital ward's staff, half of them needing a bag or a handle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half' tempts you to take half of something; instead the word itself loses its outer letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To enthral is to hold someone's attention completely, which is what a gripping story does to its reader.

clue.text: Did dock area cross delta?

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for area
to bridge a gap is to cross it
D is delta in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Did a harbour zone stretch across a river mouth?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dock' and 'delta' paint water and boats, but dock here means cut short, and the river mouth is just the letter D.
explanation.definitionFit: To dock is to cut short, as with a tail or wages; abridged means shortened, so 'did dock' fits as past tense.

clue.text: Hide from attack on small family

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece set on another comes after it, so they simply join

parts.note: to go at someone is to attack them
S is the abbreviation for small
kin are relatives

explanation.surface: Taking cover from an assault on a little household.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hide' reads as a verb, conceal yourself, but it is the noun: an animal's skin.
explanation.definitionFit: A goatskin is the skin of a goat, and an animal's skin is called its hide.

clue.text: Feature of gents' retailers?

parts.note: surface reading: something typical of men's clothing shops
setter's reading: the gents is a men's toilet, whose old cistern is flushed by pulling a hanging link; shops also form groups under one owner

explanation.walkthrough: In Britain the gents is a public men's lavatory. The answer is both the pull on an old high cistern and a group of shops under one name.
explanation.definitionFit: A pull-cord on an old toilet cistern and a group of stores under one owner share the same word.

clue.text: State of an American boxer in capsized craft

parts.note: the indefinite article
US for American

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it
a capsized boat is turned upside down, which in a down clue flips the letters

parts.note: a craft is an art or skill
Muhammad Ali, the heavyweight champion

explanation.surface: The condition of a US fighter caught in an overturned boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Craft' suggests a boat, fitting 'capsized', but it means skill, ART. 'State of' reads as condition; State alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Australia is a sovereign country, and state is a common term for a nation in that political sense.

clue.text: Not working to resolve complaint?

parts.note: to rest is to be off work
a complaint is an ailment, and to cure one is to put it right

explanation.surface: An idle employee fails to settle a grievance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Complaint' reads as a grievance, but it is an illness; the whole clue then describes the treatment as well as building it.
explanation.definitionFit: A rest cure is a treatment of prolonged inactivity and bed rest, once prescribed for nervous illnesses.

clue.text: Spur for one mostly departed

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: e.g., for example
gone, minus its final letter

explanation.surface: A spur that has largely gone missing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For one' is the crossword shorthand for 'for example', EG.
explanation.definitionFit: To spur someone is to urge them on, and egging someone on means encouraging them in the same way.

clue.text: Lack of fur, mostly, on a large puppet?

definitions.note: used adjectivally, as in a puppet ruler

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the last letter is dropped
in a down clue, one piece set on another comes after it

parts.note: no means a lack of
mink, the fur, without its last letter
taken as written
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: A big glove puppet that has lost most of its fluffy covering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Puppet' reads as a toy, but it is used like an adjective, as in a puppet government; the question mark flags the stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: A puppet leader holds a title without real power, and nominal means existing in name only.

clue.text: Stone got in your way at morning ramble's end

indicators.note: to get in is to enter, so a piece goes inside the others
at here means next to, so the pieces sit side by side

parts.note: a.m., before noon
archaic form of your
St, street, a way

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: the final letter of ramble

explanation.surface: A rock blocked a hiker's path at the end of a morning walk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stone got in your way' reads as one obstacle, but Stone is the definition and the rest is a list of pieces with the last letter of 'ramble' slotted in.
explanation.definitionFit: Amethyst is a violet variety of quartz prized as a gemstone, so it is a precious stone.

clue.text: Shelter with which to put up one in need?

parts.note: a haven is a place of shelter

indicators.note: in a down clue, putting something up raises it from the bottom, so its letters read upward

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A refuge that can house someone in trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put up' suggests giving someone lodging, matching the shelter, but in this down clue it turns the small word upward.
explanation.definitionFit: The have-nots are the poor who lack wealth or possessions, so a have-not is someone who goes without.

clue.text: Misbehave in front of petfood store

indicators.note: the front of a word is its opening letter, so that alone is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of petfood
to lay up is to store away for later

explanation.surface: Acting badly at the entrance to a pet shop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Store' reads as a shop selling petfood, but it is a verb, to lay up supplies.
explanation.definitionFit: Children who play up are being naughty or troublesome, which is the British idiom for misbehaving.

clue.text: Nancy's friends going on to make lace floor coverings

indicators.note: going on to means following next, so one piece comes after the other

parts.note: to tat is to make lace by hand
Nancy is a city in France, and amis is French for friends

explanation.surface: Nancy's pals take up lacemaking to produce rugs.
explanation.walkthrough: Nancy looks like a woman's name, but it is the French city, so her friends are in French.
explanation.definitionFit: Tatamis are the woven straw mats used to cover floors in traditional Japanese rooms.

clue.text: One's obliged by old townsperson to be silent

indicators.note: by means beside, so the pieces stand next to each other

parts.note: ta is British for thanks, what you say when obliged
cit, an old word for a citizen

explanation.surface: Someone is required by an elderly local to keep quiet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One's obliged' reads as being forced, but it is the polite phrase 'much obliged', meaning thanks; ta is the British informal thank-you.
explanation.definitionFit: Tacit means unspoken or implied without words, as in tacit agreement, so it is silent.

clue.text: Declare vests to have shrunk after spinning a few

indicators.note: spinning turns a thing round, so the letters are read backwards
shrinking leaves only part of the words, so the answer is a run of letters inside them

parts.note: a run of letters across the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: Someone announces that a handful of vests came out of the spin cycle smaller.
explanation.walkthrough: The laundry picture makes 'shrunk' and 'spinning' sound like a washing machine; both are instructions about the words 'Declare vests'.
explanation.definitionFit: Several means more than two but not many, which is close to the sense of a few.

clue.text: Star still having all-round appeal

indicators.note: all round means surrounding on every side, so one piece wraps the other

parts.note: SA, sex appeal
a still is a single photograph, a pic

explanation.surface: A celebrity who remains broadly attractive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Star' sets up a film actor with appeal, but it is a real star. 'Still' looks like an adverb but is a photo.
explanation.definitionFit: Spica is the brightest star in the constellation Virgo, so it is one of the named stars.

clue.text: State intervening in divorce, arguably with no questions asked

indicators.note: something intervening comes in between, so it sits inside another piece

parts.note: to divorce could be seen as to un-ally, undoing an alliance
a state is a condition

explanation.surface: The government stepping into a marriage split, perhaps, without any inquiry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arguably' admits that un-ally is a made-up word for divorcing, and divorces involve arguments too.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something unconditionally means without any terms or reservations, much as no questions asked suggests.

clue.text: Praises late place for Penny, returning

parts.note: late means former, as in an ex

indicators.note: returning means going back the way it came, so the letters are read in the opposite direction

parts.note: a coin goes into a slot

explanation.surface: Someone praises a departed woman named Penny as she comes back.
explanation.walkthrough: Penny looks like a name, but it is the coin, and its place is a slot in a machine.
explanation.definitionFit: To extol is to praise highly and enthusiastically, so extols matches praises as a verb.

clue.text: Shoemaker's form, when visiting doctor, is desperate

parts.note: a last is the foot-shaped block a shoe is built on

indicators.note: a visitor goes inside someone's home, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: general practitioner
as means when

explanation.surface: A cobbler's condition is critical by the time they see the doctor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Form' suggests shape or health, but a cobbler's last is a wooden foot model. A GP is a British family doctor.
explanation.definitionFit: A last-gasp effort is made at the final moment in desperation, so the compound means desperate.
